claim: Biosensors for small molecules can be used in applications that range from metabolic engineering to orthogonal control of transcription.
source: Biosensors for small molecules can be used in applications that range from metabolic engineering to orthogonal control of transcription.
evidence: This is a general statement about biosensor applications presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but supported by the overall work presented.

claim: The biosensor method is based on a ligand-binding domain (LBD) that is destabilized by mutation such that the fusion accumulates only in cells containing the target ligand.
source: The LBD is fused to either a fluorescent protein or a transcriptional activator and is destabilized by mutation such that the fusion accumulates only in cells containing the target ligand.
evidence: The mechanism is described in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with experimental data showing ligand-dependent accumulation.

claim: Biosensors for digoxin and progesterone were developed using this method.
source: We illustrate the power of this method by developing biosensors for digoxin and progesterone.
evidence: The abstract states this explicitly and the entire manuscript presents data on these two biosensors.

claim: Addition of ligand to yeast, mammalian, or plant cells expressing a biosensor activates transcription with a dynamic range of up to ~100-fold.
source: Addition of ligand to yeast, mammalian, or plant cells expressing a biosensor activates transcription with a dynamic range of up to ~100-fold.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: The biosensors were used to improve the biotransformation of pregnenolone to progesterone in yeast.
source: We use the biosensors to improve the biotransformation of pregnenolone to progesterone in yeast and to regulate CRISPR activity in mammalian cells.
evidence: This application is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The biosensors were used to regulate CRISPR activity in mammalian cells.
source: We use the biosensors to improve the biotransformation of pregnenolone to progesterone in yeast and to regulate CRISPR activity in mammalian cells.
evidence: This application is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Current biosensor construction methods typically couple binding of a small molecule to a single output signal.
source: Current methods typically couple binding of a small molecule to a single output signal, and use a limited repertoire of natural protein- (Tang et al., 2013) or nucleic acid aptamer-binding (Yang et al., 2013) domains, which narrows the scope of small molecules that can be detected.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Current biosensor methods use a limited repertoire of natural protein or nucleic acid aptamer-binding domains.
source: Current methods typically couple binding of a small molecule to a single output signal, and use a limited repertoire of natural protein- (Tang et al., 2013) or nucleic acid aptamer-binding (Yang et al., 2013) domains, which narrows the scope of small molecules that can be detected.
evidence: This statement about existing methods is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2013 and Yang et al., 2013.

claim: Conditionally stable ligand-binding domains are degraded by the ubiquitin proteasome system in the absence of a cognate ligand.
source: In the absence of a cognate ligand, these proteins are degraded by the ubiquitin proteasome system (Egeler et al., 2011).
evidence: This mechanism is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Egeler et al., 2011.

claim: Binding of the ligand stabilizes the LBD and prevents its degradation.
source: Binding of the ligand stabilizes the LBD and prevents its degradation.
evidence: This is the core mechanism described in the introduction and demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Naturally-occurring LBDs can be engineered to be conditionally stable.
source: Naturally-occurring LBDs can be engineered to be conditionally stable (Banaszynski et al., 2006; Miyazaki et al., 2012; Iwamoto et al., 2010), making it possible in principle to convert them into biosensors for target ligands.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by Banaszynski et al., 2006; Miyazaki et al., 2012; Iwamoto et al., 2010.

claim: DIG10.3 (DIG0) binds digoxin and digoxigenin with picomolar affinities.
source: We began with the computationally-designed binding domain DIG10.3 (Tinberg et al., 2013), hereafter DIG0, which binds the plant steroid glycoside digoxin and its aglycone digoxigenin with picomolar affinities.
evidence: This binding affinity is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Tinberg et al., 2013.

claim: Introduction of three rationally-designed binding site mutations into DIG0 resulted in a progesterone binder (PRO0) with nanomolar affinity.
source: Introduction of three rationally-designed binding site mutations into DIG0 resulted in a progesterone binder (PRO0) with nanomolar affinity (Tinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Tinberg et al., 2013.

claim: DIG0-GFP and PRO0-GFP fusions showed little change in fluorescence in response to digoxin or progesterone, respectively.
source: The fusions showed little change in fluorescence in response to digoxin or progesterone, respectively (Figure 1b,c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1b,c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutagenesis of LBDs can be used to identify variants that are stable only in the presence of a target ligand.
source: Work by Wandless and co-workers has shown that mutagenesis of LBDs can be used to identify variants that are stable only in the presence of a target ligand (Banaszynski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work supported by citation to Banaszynski et al., 2006.

claim: LBD variants with greater than 5-fold activation by cognate ligand were isolated after FACS sorting.
source: We isolated LBD variants having greater than 5-fold activation by cognate ligand (Figure 1b,c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1b,c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some mutations in progesterone biosensors are additive, while others predominately contribute to sensitivity.
source: By making additional variants that contain only one of the up to four mutations found in the progesterone biosensors, we showed that some mutations are additive, while others predominately contribute to sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Many of the conditionally-destabilizing mutations identified in DIG0 involve residues that participate in key dimer interface interactions.
source: Many of the conditionally-destabilizing mutations identified in DIG0 involve residues that participate in key dimer interface interactions (Figure 1d).
evidence: This structural observation is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: The conditionally-destabilizing mutations of PRO0 are located throughout the protein.
source: The conditionally-destabilizing mutations of PRO0 are located throughout the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–d)
evidence: This structural observation is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–d.

claim: DIG0 interface mutations rendered PRO0-GFP conditionally stable on binding progesterone.
source: the DIG0 interface mutations also rendered PRO0-GFP conditionally stable on binding progesterone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e.

claim: The dynamic range of TF-biosensor activity was maximal when the biosensor was expressed using a weak promoter and weak activation domain.
source: The dynamic range of TF-biosensor activity was maximal when the biosensor was expressed using a weak promoter and weak activation domain, because of lower yEGFP expression in the absence of ligand (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This optimization result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: L77F and R60S mutations in the Gal4 dimer interface increased TF-biosensor response by lowering background activity in the absence of ligand.
source: A FACS-based screen of an error-prone PCR library of G-DIG0-V, G-DIG1-V, and G-DIG2-V variants identified mutations L77F and R60S in the Gal4 dimer interface (hereafter GL77F, GR60S) that further increased TF-biosensor response by lowering background activity in the absence of ligand (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Gal4 mutations identified in digoxin-dependent TF-biosensors also increased progesterone-dependent activation of G-PRO-V biosensors.
source: Although these Gal4 mutations were identified by screening the libraries of digoxin-dependent TF-biosensors, they also increased progesterone-dependent activation of the G-PRO-V series of biosensors, indicating a shared mechanism of conditional stability in both systems (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This cross-reactivity result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Combining mutations in Gal4 and DIG0 or PRO0 led to activations of up to 60-fold by cognate ligand.
source: Combining mutations in Gal4 and DIG0 or PRO0 led to activations of up to 60-fold by cognate ligand, a ten-fold improvement over the most responsive LBD-biosensors (Figure 2c,d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2c,d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: TF-biosensors showed a five-fold increase in signal after 1 hr of incubation with ligand and full activation after ~14 hr.
source: The TF-biosensors were also rapidly activated, showing a five-fold increase in signal after 1 hr of incubation with ligand and full activation after ~14 hr (Figure 2e,f and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This kinetic result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2e,f and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: TF-biosensors exhibited a broad range of fluorescence levels across single cells and a population of nonfluorescent cells in the presence of ligand.
source: In contrast to the LBD-biosensors, the TF-biosensors exhibited a broad range of fluorescence levels across single cells, as well as a population of nonfluorescent cells in the presence of ligand (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nonfluorescent cells isolated by FACS were found to be inviable, possibly indicating plasmid loss or toxicity from biosensor activation.
source: We used FACS to isolate cells from the nonfluorescent population and found those cells to be inviable, possibly indicating plasmid loss or toxicity from biosensor activation.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text with speculation about the cause.

claim: Upon withdrawal of ligand, strains expressing TF-biosensors reached half of their maximum yEGFP fluorescence after approximately 5 hr and nearly undetectable fluorescence after 10–15 hr.
source: Upon withdrawal of ligand, strains expressing TF-biosensors rapidly exhibited reduction in signal, reaching half of their maximum yEGFP fluorescence after approximately 5 hr and nearly undetectable fluorescence after 10–15 hr (Figure 2g,h).
evidence: This kinetic result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2g,h.

claim: LexA-based TF-biosensors with DIG1 and B42 TAD showed a strong response to digoxin (nearly 40-fold) only when the promoter contained LexA-binding sites.
source: LexA-based TF-biosensors with DIG1 and a weak TAD (B42) showed a strong response to digoxin (nearly 40-fold) only when the promoter-driving reporter expression contained LexA-binding sites (Figure 3a).
evidence: This modularity result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3a.

claim: TF-biosensors drove the expression of the HIS3 reporter most effectively when steroid was added to the growth media.
source: The TF-biosensors drove the expression of the HIS3 reporter most effectively when steroid was added to the growth media, as assessed by the growth of a histidine auxotrophic strain in media lacking histidine (Figure 3b,d).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3b,d.

claim: Fusion of the Matα2 degron to the biosensor improved dynamic range by reducing the growth of yeast in the absence of ligand.
source: Fusion of the Matα2 degron to the biosensor improved dynamic range by reducing the growth of yeast in the absence of ligand.
evidence: This optimization result is stated in the text and can be inferred from the experimental design described.

claim: Deletion of the gene for a multidrug efflux pump improved biosensor sensitivity toward target ligands by increasing ligand retention.
source: Finally, the yeast strain could be modified to improve biosensor sensitivity toward target ligands by the deletion of the gene for a multidrug efflux pump (Ernst et al., 2005), thereby increasing ligand retention (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3c–d and citation to Ernst et al., 2005.

claim: TF-biosensors built from PRO1 showed the greatest dynamic range and selectivity for progesterone over pregnenolone.
source: TF-biosensors built from PRO1 showed the greatest dynamic range and selectivity for progesterone over pregnenolone when driving yEGFP expression or when coupled with a HIS3 reporter assay (Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: GL77F-PRO1-V biosensor could detect progesterone production, with biosensor response greatest when 3β-HSD was expressed from a high copy number plasmid and from a strong promoter.
source: Using GL77F-PRO1-V driving a yEGFP reporter, we could detect progesterone production, with biosensor response greatest when 3β-HSD was expressed from a high copy number plasmid and from a strong promoter (Figure 4d).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4d.

claim: Two evolved 3β-HSD mutants, N139D and F67Y, produced two-fold more progesterone per OD than cells bearing the wild-type enzyme.
source: Two of the mutants, 3β-HSD N139D and 3β-HSD F67Y, were assayed for progesterone production using gas chromatography and mass spectrometry and were found to produce two-fold more progesterone per OD than cells bearing the wild-type enzyme (Figure 4f).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4f.

claim: Human K562 cells demonstrated greater sensitivity to digoxin, with fluorescence activation increasing up to 100 nM of cognate ligand for digoxin biosensors and 1 mM for progesterone biosensors.
source: As with yeast, the human cells demonstrated greater sensitivity to digoxin, with fluorescence activation increasing up to 100 nM of cognate ligand for digoxin biosensors and 1 mM for progesterone biosensors.
evidence: This result is stated in the text describing mammalian cell experiments.

claim: Greater than 100-fold activation was observed for the most sensitive progesterone biosensor GL77F-PRO1-V in mammalian cells.
source: We observed >100-fold activation for the most sensitive progesterone biosensor GL77F-PRO1-V.
evidence: This result is stated in the text describing mammalian cell experiments.

claim: The increase in mammalian dynamic range over yeast may arise from more aggressive degradation of destabilized biosensors or greater accumulation of target-stabilized biosensors or reporters resulting from larger cell sizes and slower doubling times.
source: The increase in mammalian dynamic range over yeast may arise from more aggressive degradation of destabilized biosensors or greater accumulation of target-stabilized biosensors or reporters resulting from larger cell sizes and slower doubling times.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in dynamic range between yeast and mammalian cells.

claim: Fluorescence increased four-fold within 4 hr of target introduction and rose logarithmically for 24–48 hr in mammalian cells.
source: The time course data show that fluorescence increased four-fold within 4 hr of target introduction and rose logarithmically for 24–48 hr.
evidence: This kinetic result is stated in the text describing mammalian cell experiments.

claim: Unchecked Cas9 activity can lead to off-target mutations and cytotoxicity.
source: Despite the high programmability and specificity of Cas9-mediated gene editing achieved to date, unchecked Cas9 activity can lead to off-target mutations and cytotoxicity (Fu et al., 2013; Mali et al., 2013; Pattanayak et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement about CRISPR/Cas9 is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2013; Mali et al., 2013; Pattanayak et al., 2013.

claim: An ~18-fold increase in GFP positive cells with digoxigenin relative to the mock control was observed using DIG-Cas9 fusions.
source: After a 48-hr incubation period, we observed an ~18-fold increase in GFP positive cells with digoxigenin relative to the mock control (Figure 5e).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5e.

claim: The biosensor containing the Matα2 degron and VP16 TAD showed the highest fold activation of luciferase in the presence of digoxigenin in Arabidopsis protoplasts.
source: The biosensor containing the Matα2 degron and VP16 TAD showed the highest fold activation of luciferase in the presence of digoxigenin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: After 42 hr, 30-50-fold induction of luciferase activity was observed in digoxin-treated Arabidopsis plants compared to the uninduced control.
source: After 42 hr, we observed 30-50-fold induction of luciferase activity in digoxin-treated plants compared to the uninduced control (Figure 6).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Both digoxin and digoxigenin were capable of inducing the biosensor in Arabidopsis plants.
source: Both digoxin and digoxigenin were capable of inducing the biosensor.
evidence: This result is stated in the text describing plant experiments.

claim: Digoxigenin-dependent luciferase induction was observed in multiple independent transgenic T1 lines.
source: Digoxigenin-dependent luciferase induction was observed in multiple independent transgenic T1 lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A rising dose response to digoxigenin was observed in the transgenic Arabidopsis plants.
source: and a rising dose response to digoxigenin was observed in the transgenic plants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The specificity of the digoxigenin biosensor in plants parallels that in yeast cells.
source: The specificity of the digoxigenin biosensor in plants parallels that in yeast cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The majority of the conditionally-stabilizing mutations are located at the dimer interfaces of both the DIG0 LBD and Gal4.
source: Both the DIG0 LBD and Gal4 are homodimers, and the majority of the conditionally-stabilizing mutations are located at the dimer interfaces.
evidence: This structural observation is stated in the Discussion and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: A computational model of the Gal4-DIG0 complex indicates that the orientation of the two domains allows a homodimeric fusion to form.
source: A computational model of the Gal4-DIG0 complex indicates that the orientation of the two domains allows a homodimeric fusion to form (Figure 2b).
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: Weakening of the dimer interface, in either the DIG0 or the Gal4 domain, is compensated by ligand binding.
source: These results suggest an allosteric interplay between ligand binding and dimer formation: weakening of the dimer interface, in either the DIG0 or the Gal4 domain, is compensated by ligand binding.
evidence: This mechanistic interpretation is stated in the Discussion based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The DIG0 LBD scaffold is derived from a member of the nuclear transport factor 2 family.
source: This LBD scaffold is derived from a member of the nuclear transport factor 2 family, a fold class that typically has a large dimer interface (~1200 Å2) that facilitates the large and open ligand-binding site (~600 Å2).
evidence: This structural information is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Nuclear transport factor 2 family proteins typically have a large dimer interface (~1200 Å2) and a large and open ligand-binding site (~600 Å2).
source: This LBD scaffold is derived from a member of the nuclear transport factor 2 family, a fold class that typically has a large dimer interface (~1200 Å2) that facilitates the large and open ligand-binding site (~600 Å2).
evidence: This structural information is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Nuclear transport factor 2 family proteins are well suited for de novo design of LBDs because of their large binding pocket and natural substrate diversity.
source: These protein folds are well suited for de novo design of other LBDs because of their large binding pocket and natural substrate diversity (Todd et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is made in the Discussion and supported by citation to Todd et al., 2002.

claim: Exploiting dimer interfaces to modulate stability without impairing ligand binding may be a general mechanism to confer conditional stability on LBDs.
source: Exploiting dimer interfaces to modulate stability without impairing ligand binding may be a general mechanism to confer conditional stability on LBDs.
evidence: This is a generalization proposed in the Discussion based on the results presented.

claim: Interface mutations in DIG0 and Gal4 conferring digoxin-dependent stability lead to progesterone-dependent stability in a progesterone biosensor.
source: This possibility is supported by the observation that interface mutations in DIG0 and Gal4 conferring digoxin-dependent stability lead to progesterone-dependent stability in a progesterone biosensor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This observation is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Transcriptional control by a product or intermediate has emerged as a promising strategy for metabolic engineering.
source: Transcriptional control by a product or intermediate (Zhang et al., 2012; Raman et al., 2014; Tang and Cirino, 2011) and directed evolution of constituent pathway elements (Agresti et al., 2010; Alper et al., 2005; Dietrich et al., 2013) have emerged as promising strategies towards this goal.
evidence: This statement about metabolic engineering strategies is supported by multiple citations.

claim: These biosensor approaches require high selectivity against intermediates.
source: These approaches require high selectivity against intermediates (Zhang and Keasling, 2011), a feature demonstrated here that can be explicitly considered during the computational design and screening process.
evidence: This requirement is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Zhang and Keasling, 2011.

claim: The biosensors required only minimal modifications to retain high levels of sensitivity when developed in yeast and deployed across mammalian and plant species.
source: Here, we engineered biosensors based on a designed scaffold derived from a bacterial protein. These biosensors required only minimal modifications to retain high levels of sensitivity when developed in yeast and deployed across mammalian and plant species, demonstrating unprecedented portability for biosensors.
evidence: This portability result is stated in the Discussion and supported by the experimental data across different organisms.

claim: In some cases, these biosensors showed a greater dynamic range in mammalian cells relative to yeast, possibly due to larger cell volume and variations in protein degradation machinery.
source: In some cases, these biosensors showed a greater dynamic range in mammalian cells relative to yeast, possibly due to larger cell volume and variations in protein degradation machinery.
evidence: This observation is stated in the Discussion with speculation about the cause.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 system can result in off-target genetic changes.
source: The CRISPR/Cas9 system provides a facile and robust genome-editing platform, but it can result in off-target genetic changes (Fu et al., 2013; Mali et al., 2013; Pattanayak et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement about CRISPR/Cas9 is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2013; Mali et al., 2013; Pattanayak et al., 2013.

claim: Small molecule inducers including doxycycline and rapamycin may confer leaky expression and cytotoxicity.
source: While small molecule inducers including doxycycline and rapamycin have been used, these molecules may confer leaky expression and cytotoxicity (Xie et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement about existing inducers is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2008.

claim: By exploiting the low background of the LBD-biosensors, biosensor-Cas9 fusions with tightly controlled activation were produced.
source: By exploiting the low background of the LBD-biosensors, we produced biosensor-Cas9 fusions with tightly controlled activation (Figure 5e).
evidence: This result is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 5e.

claim: Switch-like control over CRISPR/Cas9 activity could reduce background activity and off-target editing.
source: This switch-like control over CRISPR/Cas9 activity could reduce background activity and off-target editing, a critical feature for safer gene therapies (Mandal, et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2013; Schwank et al., 2013).
evidence: This potential application is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Mandal, et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2013; Schwank et al., 2013.

claim: In the transgenic Arabidopsis plants, ligand-dependent activation was observed in all cells, tissues and organs examined.
source: In the transgenic Arabidopsis plants, we observed ligand-dependent activation in all cells, tissues and organs examined (Figure 6).
evidence: This observation is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The generality of the biosensor approach arises from the universality of the transcriptional activation and protein degradation machinery across eukaryotes, together with the modularity and tunability of the constituent parts.
source: The generality of our approach arises from the universality of the transcriptional activation and protein degradation machinery across eukaryotes, together with the modularity and tunability of the constituent parts.
evidence: This explanation for the generality of the method is stated in the Discussion based on the overall results.

claim: Error-prone PCR of DIG10.3 showed a mutation rate of 0–7 mutations/kb.
source: Sanger sequencing of 16 colonies showed a mutation rate of 0–7 mutations/kb.
evidence: This result is stated in the Materials and methods section describing library construction.

claim: Libraries of DIG0-yEGFP and PRO0-yEGFP were subjected to three rounds of fluorescence activated sorting.
source: Libraries of DIG0-yEGFP and PRO0-yEGFP integrated into yeast strain Y7092 were subject to three rounds of fluorescence activated sorting in a BD FACSAria IIu.
evidence: This experimental procedure is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In the first round of FACS, cells showing the top 5% of fluorescence activation in the presence of steroid were collected.
source: For the first round, cells were grown overnight to an OD600 of ~1.0 in YPAD containing steroid (500 μM digoxigenin or 50 μM progesterone), and cells showing the top 5% of fluorescence activation were collected
evidence: This experimental procedure is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In the second sort, cells displaying the lowest ~3% fluorescence activation in the absence of steroid were collected.
source: In the second sort, cells displaying the lowest ~3% fluorescence activation were collected.
evidence: This experimental procedure is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A computational model of the Gal4-DIG10.3 fusion was built using Rosetta Remodel.
source: A model of the Gal4-DIG10.3 fusion was built using Rosetta Remodel (Huang et al., 2011) to assess whether the linker between Gal4 and the DIG LBD, which are both dimers, would allow for the formation of a dimer in the fusion construct.
evidence: This computational method is described in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Huang et al., 2011.

claim: The lowest energy model of the Gal4-DIG fusion satisfied the dimer constraints, indicating that a homodimer configuration of the fusion is possible.
source: The lowest energy model satisfied the dimer constraints, indicating that a homodimer configuration of the fusion is possible.
evidence: This computational result is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Progesterone became toxic at levels of 100 μM and above, leading to substantial cell death.
source: Progesterone became toxic at levels of 100 μM and above, leading to substantial cell death.
evidence: This observation is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4.

claim: Beta-estradiol and hydrocortisone were not soluble in yeast growth media at levels above 25 μM.
source: β-estradiol and hydrocortisone were not soluble in yeast growth media at levels above 25 μM.
evidence: This observation is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4.

claim: The K562 cell line was obtained from the ATCC.
source: The K562 cell line was obtained from the ATCC.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The K562 cell line was not authenticated and not tested for mycoplasma contamination.
source: The cell line was not authenticated and not tested for mycoplasma contamination.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
